lesson.grammar_point: relative clauses with who, which, that and where

listenings.text: Luiz, it's Diane. I am sending you the sheet that we give new colleagues, and it is not the organisation chart. Ana is the one in legal who approves without going up, and she has been there nineteen years. Marco is the representative who knows every dealer in the north personally. The south is the region where most of the volume sits, which is why everybody calls you. And the last line is the one that people ignore. At the harvest dinner, ask about the soil. Two hours, guaranteed.

Luiz, Tom Baker. You asked me at dinner which region the wine came from, and I did not have a good answer, so here is the one I got. The man who poured it said it is almost never the grape. It is the place where the grape grows: the soil, the height, and the month that it rains. He said the region that everybody names is usually the one which markets itself best. Ask your growers the same question about soil. You will get the same answer.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: a person who speaks and acts for a company with its customers
a field where grapes are grown
the one person the other side should call first
a large separate part of a company, with its own management
the earth a plant grows in, and what it gives the fruit
a whole part of the economy, such as farming or banking
somebody who knows one narrow thing extremely well
the chain that says who answers to whom

paras: On your first day you are handed a chart with two hundred names on it, and within a month you discover that it answers a question nobody actually asks. The chart tells you who reports to whom. What you need to know is who is the person who can answer this in four minutes instead of three weeks, which region is the one where most of the volume sits, and which colleague is the one everybody quietly calls before a decision goes up. That second map is never written down, and building it is most of what the first year in a big organisation really consists of.

Describing that map to somebody else is a language problem before it is anything else, because every useful sentence in it has the same shape. The analyst who handles the south. The division which was created two years ago. The region where the volume sits. A short clause hangs off a noun and tells you which one is meant, and without it you are left with names and titles that carry no information. It is the difference between saying that Ana is a specialist and saying that Ana is the specialist who has been in the legal division for nineteen years and who can approve this without going upstairs.

The same shape does something else, and it is not a coincidence. Ask anybody who knows about wine what makes a region, and the answer comes out in exactly this form: a valley where the days are hot and the nights are cold, a soil which holds water badly, families who cannot afford to make a wine that tastes like everybody else's. Places and people are described in the same way because in both cases the point is the same: not the name, but which one, and why that matters. Learn the structure once and you can introduce a colleague, explain a company, or describe a vineyard, without ever sounding like a list.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: Organisation charts should be redrawn so that they show who is useful.
What you really need is a second, unwritten map of who does what, and describing it — like describing a wine region — needs one particular sentence shape.
Wine regions and companies are difficult to describe because both are complicated.
